newsitem.title: JAPAN: Fears of Japan E.coli epidemic after new outbreak.
newsitem.headline: Fears of Japan E.coli epidemic after new outbreak.

text.p: Government officials said on Thursday that 58 people at a hospital in western Japan had been infected with a deadly strain of the E. coli bacteria responsible for a rash of food poisoning deaths last year.
Those infected include 41 student nurses, 16 patients and one other staff member at Okayama Rosai Hospital, who all ate the same meal on Monday, an official of the Okayama city government said.

He said five of those infected, all of them patients at the hospital, had severe cases of bloody diarrhoea, considered a serious symptom in the potentially fatal disease caused by the O-157 E. coli bacteria.
"We have stopped meals at the hospital and are trying to prevent further spread of the disease while we determine the exact source of the infection," he said.
The new outbreak has raised fears of a return of the deadly food poisoning epidemic in Japan last summer that killed 11 people and made more than 10,000 ill.
"With only isolated cases of the strain since January this year, we thought the trend had calmed down," a spokesman for the Health and Welfare Ministry said.
"But with the rainy season on us and summer beginning to hot up, it is a time when the human body gets weaker and the bacteria begin to multiply faster."
The western city of Sakai, near Osaka in western Japan, was hit hardest by last summer's outbreak, with more than 6,500 people affected in the area, mainly schoolchildren.
The ministry could not determine the exact source of the injection but pointed to radish sprouts as a possible cause of the outbreak.
The Okayama outbreak comes after health authorities in Hong Kong discovered the deadly microbe in beef on sale in a Japanese supermarket in May, following an earlier case in the territory in March.
Last year, the strain killed 20 people in Scotland and several people in the United States and Canada.
The deadliest single outbreak of the E. coli strain was in Canada, where 19 elderly people infected in a nursing home died in September 1985.

O-157 is commonly spread through human or animal waste, contamination of meat, vegetables, dairy products and water and is recognised as one of the fastest-growing food-borne infectious diseases in the world.
